opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about almost every day. With a team that size, the hardest part isn't the technical problems; it's making sure everyone is rowing in the same direction.

The first thing is a very clear north star. For Cosmos, the goal is to build world foundation models that help physical AI, like robots and autonomous vehicles, understand and simulate the physical world. Everything we do has to connect back to that. When someone proposes a new direction, the first question is: does this help physical AI developers? If the answer is fuzzy, we probably shouldn't do it, at least not now.

The second thing is turning that north star into something concrete and measurable. "Better world model" means nothing to an engineer on a Tuesday afternoon. So we define what better means: physical plausibility, controllability, how useful the model is for downstream tasks like policy learning or synthetic data generation. Once we agree on the evaluations, a lot of debates resolve themselves. People can disagree about methods, but the numbers tell us what's working.

Third, I try to keep the structure simple. We break the team into groups with clear ownership: data, model architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, evaluation, and so on. Each group has a lead who can make decisions without escalating everything to me. If every decision has to come to one person, you become the bottleneck and the team slows down. My job is more to set priorities, resolve conflicts between groups, and make the calls that are truly cross-cutting.

And then there's communication. We have regular syncs where the groups share progress, and I push people to share failures early, not just successes. In research, a lot of things don't work. If someone spends three weeks on something that's a dead end and nobody knows, that's a waste. If they say after three days, "this isn't working, here's why," the whole team learns.

Finally, I think culture matters a lot. I want people to feel ownership, like this is their model, not my model. When people feel that, they make good decisions on their own, because they care about the outcome. And honestly, at NVIDIA we have a lot of very talented people. My job is less to tell them what to do and more to give them context so they can make the right call themselves.

It's not perfect. There are always tensions, like research exploration versus shipping on time, or one group's needs versus another's. But having a shared goal, shared metrics, and a lot of transparency gets you most of the way there.

r002.rationale: It explains that a shared north star gives team members a basis for evaluating directions and making decisions that serve the team’s goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'll say is that you don't really "help" 200 people make decisions. If I had to be involved in every decision, we would have failed already. So the real question is how you set things up so most decisions get made without me, and still point the same way.

The way I think about it is in a few layers.

The first layer is the mission, and it has to be simple enough that you can say it in one sentence. For Cosmos, that sentence is basically: build the world foundation model that lets physical AI — robots, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to act in the real world — learn and be tested in simulation. If everyone on the team can say that sentence and actually believe it, then a lot of small decisions become obvious. If you're a researcher deciding whether to spend a month on a benchmark, you ask: does this help a robot developer? If not, probably don't do it.

The second layer is a small number of very concrete goals for the current cycle. For Cosmos 3 we had maybe three or four. Things like the physics fidelity we needed, the control interface we needed to support, the inference cost we had to hit so people could actually deploy it. I try to be very explicit about priority ordering, because the real conflicts come when two good goals fight each other. If I just say "all of these matter," I've pushed the decision back to the person, and they'll resolve it differently from the person sitting next to them.

The third layer is how the team is organized. 200 people is really maybe fifteen or twenty groups. Data, pre-training, post-training, evaluation, infrastructure, the applied teams working with robotics customers. Each group has a lead, and the leads own their domain. My job with the leads is mostly to make sure the interfaces between groups are clear — what does the data team promise the training team, what does the training team promise the applied team. Most of the painful misalignment I've seen isn't inside a group, it's at the boundaries.

Then there's a cultural piece, which I think is maybe the most important and the hardest to describe. We try to make disagreement cheap and public. If someone thinks a direction is wrong, they should say so in the channel where the decision is being made, not in a hallway afterwards. And we try to decide with evidence. In this field you can argue forever about whether an approach will work, or you can run the experiment and look at the number. We bias very hard toward running the experiment. That resolves a lot of debates, and it also means I don't have to be the tiebreaker as often, because the data is the tiebreaker.

And I'll admit I do a lot of repeating myself. I say the same mission, the same priorities, in the all-hands, in one-on-ones, in reviews. It feels redundant to me, but with a team this size, every time you say it, there's someone hearing it for the first time, or someone who had drifted and needed to hear it again.

Where I actually get involved personally is a short list. Decisions that change the architecture of the model. Decisions about what we release and how. And decisions where two groups genuinely can't agree and it's blocking them. Everything else I try to stay out of, even when I have an opinion. Sometimes that's uncomfortable, because you see someone going down a path you wouldn't have chosen. But if you override every one of those, people stop deciding, and then you really are the bottleneck for 200 people.

r001.rationale: The response describes a clear mission but does not say that the vision may differ from the eventual model.

r002.rationale: It says a shared mission makes individual decisions clearer and gives a researcher’s decision as an example of checking whether work helps the team’s goal.

astra-6.text:
For a team that size, I think the key is shared context. People need to understand what we’re trying to achieve, why it matters, and how we’ll judge whether we’re making progress. If that’s clear, they can make decisions without everything coming back to one person.

I’d separate the goal from the approach. We need alignment on the goal, but we should leave room for people to challenge the approach. When there’s a disagreement, the useful question is: which choice gets us closer to the outcome we care about, and what evidence would help us decide?

And that takes repetition. You can’t communicate the direction once and assume everyone has the same understanding. You have to keep connecting individual decisions back to the larger goal, while listening for places where that goal is unclear.

r001.rationale: The response does not say whether the communicated vision needs to match the eventual model.

r002.rationale: It says a clear shared goal and outcome let team members make decisions independently while connecting those decisions to the larger goal.

sol-6.1.text:
For a team that large, I think the key is to align on the goal without trying to make every decision centrally. People need to understand what we’re trying to achieve, why it matters, and how we’ll know we’re making progress. Then each team needs enough ownership to decide how to contribute.

The difficult part is that alignment isn’t something you communicate once. Different teams will encounter different tradeoffs. When those come up, you have to bring the discussion back to the shared goal: does this choice move us closer, and what evidence do we have? If people share that framework, they can make decisions independently and still move in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses aligning around a shared goal, but does not say the communicated vision may differ from the eventual model.

r002.rationale: It says understanding the shared goal and using it to assess tradeoffs lets teams decide independently while moving in the same direction.
